title: Mexico Sees the US as a ‘Greater Threat’ Than China or Russia, New Survey Confirms
author: SinEmbargo Editorial Staff
content:
_This article originally appeared in the[September 20, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4872309/mexico-ve-a-eu-como-una-mayor-
amenaza-que-china-o-rusia-confirma-nueva-encuesta/), a Mexican independent
digital news outlet._

**Mexico City, September 20 (SinEmbargo).—** The United States is seen by
Mexicans as a much greater threat to Mexico than China or Russia. A survey
conducted by Focaldata for the Rockefeller Foundation reveals that **58
percent** of those consulted consider that the US government represents a
major threat to the country, a perception that **practically doubles the one
recorded for China, at 27 percent** , and far exceeds Russia, at 34 percent.

The result contrasts with a purported survey released days earlier by
NewsNation and reproduced by various Mexican media outlets, according to which
a majority of Mexicans would support direct US actions against the cartels,
including operations carried out on national territory without prior notice to
the Mexican government. Unlike the Focaldata study, which identifies the
universe of countries, the fieldwork period, and the sample size, NewsNation
did not publish the full document it attributed to the State Department, nor
did it identify the company that supposedly interviewed a thousand Mexicans,
nor did it reveal the questions, the specific percentages, the fieldwork
dates, the sample selection method, or the margin of error.

By contrast, the Focaldata survey data places Washington —Mexico's main
trading partner and its immediate neighbor— as the country that generates the
most concern among Mexicans out of the powers evaluated. The result is part of
an international study applied in 34 countries to measure perceptions of the
world scenario, external threats, security priorities, international
cooperation, and economic expectations. The fieldwork was carried out between
July 21 and August 5, 2026, and gathered the responses of 35,399 people
through nationally representative surveys.

In the Mexican case, the difference is particularly wide. The United States
records **a lead of 31 percentage points over China** as a major threat, and
24 points over Russia. The result places Mexico within a group of developing
countries where the United States appears more frequently as a major threat
than the other two major powers analyzed.

The survey did not ask people to directly rank the United States, China, and
Russia from greatest to least threat. Instead, participants evaluated
separately whether each one represented a major threat, a minor threat, or no
threat to their country. For that reason, the percentages reflect the
perception of each power independently.

![Chart: share of Mexicans who see the US, China, and Russia as a major
threat](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/02-us-threat-
chart-1.jpg)Mexico stands out among the countries where the US is perceived as
a greater threat than China and Russia: 58% of Mexicans surveyed named the US,
versus 27% who named China and 34% Russia. Chart recreated and translated into
Spanish by SinEmbargo using AI, based on the original.

**Fifty-eight percent of the Mexicans consulted identified the United States
as a major threat** , compared to the 34 percent who pointed to Russia and the
27 percent who did the same with China. The difference among the three powers
is also part of a broader trend recorded in developing economies.

According to the study, the United States was identified as the greatest
threat of the three powers in **12 of the 16 developing countries** included
in the survey. By contrast, this occurred in only two of the 16 economies
considered wealthier: Canada and Singapore.

The perception recorded in Mexico is also among the highest in the study. The
percentage of people who consider the United States a major threat reaches
**73 percent in Indonesia, 59 percent in Brazil, 58 percent in Mexico, and 57
percent in Turkey**.

The Mexican result is also part of a regional trend. The survey notes that
**all the Latin American countries included in the study** , like the
countries of the Middle East, North Africa, and Turkey region, rated the
United States as a greater threat than Russia or China.

![Vladimir Putin alongside Donald Trump](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/03-putin-trump.jpg)Vladimir Putin, President of
Russia, alongside Donald Trump, President of the United States. Photo: White
House.

The situation contrasts with the perception of China in some Asian countries.
The study found that concern over Beijing is concentrated particularly in
countries in its vicinity: 70 percent of those surveyed in the Philippines
considered China a major threat, as did 67 percent in Japan, 62 percent in
South Korea, 48 percent in India, and 47 percent in Australia.

Globally, Russia obtained the highest median proportion of people who consider
it a major threat, at 42 percent, followed by the United States at 34 percent
and China at 30 percent. However, the distribution changes considerably across
countries and regions.

This past July, a report published by the Pew Research Center revealed that
the perception of China and its President, Xi Jinping, has improved
considerably in recent years in Mexico and Canada, the two main allies and
trading partners of the United States.

This shift has been recorded particularly during the second term of President
Donald Trump, to the point that the image of the Asian country is now more
favorable globally than that of the United States. In Mexico and Canada, in
fact, China receives a more positive rating and Xi Jinping generates higher
levels of trust than the US president.

Now the Focaldata study notes that there is no power that is uniformly
considered the main threat throughout the world. Nonetheless, the United
States appears as the greatest threat among the three powers in 14 of the 32
countries where it was possible to compare the three perceptions, while Russia
holds that position in 14 countries and China in five.

In 22 of the 32 countries that evaluated both the United States and China,
moreover, a greater proportion of people considered the North American country
a major threat. The median difference was 12 percentage points. Among the
wealthier economies the result was split, while in 14 of the 16 developing
economies the United States was cited more frequently than China.

![Chart: how people in 36 countries view the US and
China](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/04-us-china-
favorability.jpg)How people in 36 countries view the US and China (% with a
favorable opinion). Source: Pew Research Center. Chart in Spanish, as
published by SinEmbargo.

The perception of international threats is accompanied by a change in security
priorities. Worldwide, avoiding wars and conflicts became one of the main
concerns of respondents.

Forty-four percent of the people consulted in the 34 countries placed the
prevention of wars and conflicts among their top three priorities. The issue
ranked first in 21 countries and was among the top two priorities in 33 of the
34 countries included in the study.

In Mexico, the proportion increased nine percentage points compared to the
measurement carried out in November 2025. **It went from 33 to 42 percent**
between the two measurements, according to the report.

The increase places the prevention of wars and conflicts as one of the issues
that gained the most importance for Mexicans within the set of international
priorities considered by the survey.

In developing economies, the study found that, in addition to avoiding wars
and conflicts, there is considerable concern about international economic
conditions. Forty-two percent indicated that among their main priorities are a
fairer world economy and trade, while 41 percent mentioned the prevention of
wars and conflicts.

Other issues had lower percentages: reducing poverty was mentioned by 27
percent, humanitarian aid by 27 percent, democracy and human rights by 25
percent, climate change by 25 percent, and access to food and drinking water
by 23 percent. Migration was cited by 10 percent.

The study also asked who should take a central role in preventing wars. Across
the surveyed countries, groups of countries working together were most
frequently considered the appropriate actors to address this type of problem.
This option was chosen by 45 percent in the wealthier economies and by 38
percent in the developing economies, above the percentages recorded for
national governments.

![Chart: share of Mexicans ranking war prevention among top global
problems](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/05-mexico-
war-priority-chart.jpg)In Mexico, the share of people who ranked the
prevention of wars and conflicts among the top three global problems rose from
33% to 42% between late 2025 and July–August 2026. Chart recreated and
translated into Spanish by SinEmbargo using AI, based on the original.

Despite the perception of a more conflict-ridden international scenario, the
survey found that the majority of participants continue to support cooperation
among countries.

Globally, 57 percent of respondents said they would support their country
cooperating with other governments to solve international problems, even if
that meant compromising some national interests. The figure rose from 55
percent in the previous measurement.

Among developing economies, support was 53 percent. In Mexico, by contrast,
the proportion was 50 percent, four percentage points less than in the
previous measurement.

The report notes that there is an even greater willingness when international
cooperation is directly linked to concrete results. Eighty-one percent of
respondents worldwide said they would support cooperation more if it
demonstrated that it can solve global problems, while 80 percent indicated
they would back it more if it could show that it helps solve problems within
their own country.

The study also raised the possibility of a group of countries working together
to address global problems without including either the United States or
China. **Sixty-one percent of respondents supported that possibility** ,
compared to 12 percent who were against it. Support was similar among the
wealthier economies, at 60 percent, and the developing economies, at 62
percent.

The results thus show that the perception of the major powers does not
necessarily translate into a rejection of international cooperation. On the
contrary, a majority of respondents maintain their support for working with
other countries, although the support is related to the expectation that such
cooperation produces concrete results.
